verdict.reasoning: Patient reports: "I've been having a cough and a sore throat, for about a week" and confirms sore throat came first then cough; cough described as "very dry."
Patient states: "today's Friday, sore throat was about, last week, Friday or Thursday."
Patient: "the, sore throat came first, and then, after a day or two, the cough" and later ties cough to Saturday or Sunday after Thurs/Fri sore throat.
Patient says shortness of breath started "shortly after the cough. So maybe a day or two later. So, three, four days ago." Doctor repeats "Three or four days ago, you started develop..."

Cough is "very dry"; patient says it's "the same throughout the whole day" when asked if worse at night. Doctor: "you're not coughing up any flem?" and later "you're not coughing up blood"; both implied no sputum/hemoptysis.

Patient: shortness of breath occurs "when I'm doing walking"; can still exercise: "hasn't stopped me from doing any of those things" and is described as "pretty unusual, and a little bit worrying," indicating mild exertional SOB.
Doctor asks: "do you have any wheeze? Or chest pain?" Patient: "uh, yeah, a bit of both"; doctor summarizes: "you're feeling a bit wheezy, with some chest pain as well."
Patient: "a little bit feverish... at first. So the first three or so days of this, but then it, the fever's gone away."
Patient: "also had a bit of a headache. But like, headaches that come and go rather, but like, right now it's fine."
Patient: "no weight loss, but I have been, have been losing my appetite recently" and confirms no weight loss: "No. Not that..."

For nasal/sinus: Patient says symptoms are "entirely with just my throat. So like, my nose is like" implying no congestion. For rashes, doctor asks "any, um, sort of rashes or anything?" Patient: "No."
Doctor: "do you have any other medical conditions, or medical history?" Patient: "No, just, no, no, past medical history, no."
Patient: "Well, my mother had lung cancer." Doctor repeats: "Your mother had lung cancer."
Doctor: "are you taking any medications, currently, at the moment?" Patient: "No, no."
Patient: "Not to any medication, but I'm allergic to peanuts." Doctor repeats: "Peanuts. OK."

Non-smoker: Doctor: "Do you smoke?" Patient: "No."; "Ever smoked?" Patient: "once or twice in Amsterdam... but, not really." Place of birth and residence: Patient: "I was born in the US, and moved over... it was twelve years ago."
Patient: "in terms of recent travel. Just to Europe, nowhere too exotic." Doctor: "no significant recent travel any, anywhere."

Patient: "I've had to stay away from work, for about three or four of those days" and later requests "maybe even a sick note. So that, if I need to stay away from work for a bit longer, I can get one."
The transcript describes symptoms but no explicit diagnostic label such as "acute viral upper respiratory tract infection" or "pharyngitis" is stated.
Patient: "I've had to stay away from work, for about three or four of those days" and later: "I stayed home from work two days this week."
History of peanut allergy is documented: "Not to any medication, but I'm allergic to peanuts."
Doctor: "I expect this to sort of be getting better in the next, four or five days" and advises: "paracetemol. Lots of fluids. Um, and, uh, rest up."

Doctor advises seeking GP care if more short of breath or if not better in 4–5 days, but does not mention emergency care, new/worsening chest pain, or fever recurrence: "If you feel significantly worse... more short of breath... then I would advise you to... go and see a GP" and "if it's not [better in 4–5 days], please get in touch with a medical professional again."
Doctor: "I'll provide you with a sick note, just to give you a few more days off work."
While peanut allergy is noted, there is no advice in the transcript about continued avoidance of peanuts or carrying emergency medications.
